lead: Quantization rounds each sample to one of L allowed levels. In a uniform quantizer the levels are equally spaced by Δ, so every sample carries the same worst-case error. Speech has small samples far more often than large ones, so uniform steps waste resolution on quiet passages and clip loud peaks. Non-uniform quantization gives fine steps near zero and coarse steps at high amplitude; companding is the practical way to get this. Telephone PCM, VoIP and audio codecs use these ideas.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.1 for sampling, and Unit 1 for random variables and noise power.

blocks.text: A quantizer maps a continuous sample x to the nearest of L discrete levels. When the step between neighbouring levels is the same everywhere, the quantizer is uniform. For an n-bit code, L = 2ⁿ. If the full-scale range is from −V to +V, the total width is 2V, so the step is Δ = 2V / L. Each sample is replaced by the level closest to it; the difference is the quantization error e = q(x) − x.
Δ = 2V / L,  L = 2ⁿ,  −Δ/2 ≤ e ≤ Δ/2,  P<sub>q</sub> = Δ²/12
blocks.where: V is the maximum input magnitude in volts; L is the number of levels; n is the number of bits per sample; Δ is the step in volts; e is quantization error in volts; P<sub>q</sub> is quantization noise power in V², for a uniformly distributed error.

blocks.text: For a smooth signal and a fine step, e is almost uniformly spread over one step, so its mean is zero and its power is Δ²/12. This is granular noise: it exists even when the channel is perfect. A sample outside ±V is clipped to the end level, giving overload distortion. Overload is not included in Δ²/12.

The signal-to-quantization-noise ratio for a full-scale sinusoid x(t) = V sin(2πft) is SQNR = (V²/2) / (Δ²/12). Substituting Δ = 2V/2ⁿ gives SQNR = (3/2)2²ⁿ, or in decibels SQNR = 6.02n + 1.76 dB. Each extra bit adds about 6 dB. This formula assumes the sine uses the full range; a quiet talker gets much less.

blocks.where: SQNR<sub>dB</sub> is the signal-to-quantization-noise ratio in decibels for a full-scale sinusoid; n is bits per sample. For other signals use 10 log₁₀(P<sub>signal</sub> / P<sub>q</sub>).

blocks.text: Uniform steps give the same absolute error at all amplitudes. Speech statistics are closer to logarithmic: quiet sounds need small absolute error to sound clean, loud sounds can tolerate larger error. A non-uniform quantizer uses small Δ near zero and larger Δ at large |x|. The step size becomes a function of x, so P<sub>q</sub> is not simply Δ²/12 with one Δ.

Companding means compressing at the transmitter and expanding at the receiver. A compander is the pair: compressor before the uniform quantizer, expander after reconstruction. The compressor y = C(x) boosts small inputs, so after uniform quantization the small inputs have effectively finer steps. The expander applies C⁻¹. In telephony the compressor is a smooth curve, implemented by a segmented approximation in PCM chips.
y = sgn(x) · ln(1 + μ|x|/V) / ln(1 + μ),  |x| ≤ V
blocks.where: x is the input sample in volts; V is full scale; y is the normalized compressed output; sgn(x) is +1 for x > 0 and −1 for x < 0; μ controls the amount of compression. μ = 255 is standard for 8-bit speech PCM in North America and Japan.

blocks.text: y = sgn(x) · A|x|/V / (1 + ln A)  for |x|/V ≤ 1/A;  y = sgn(x) · (1 + ln(A|x|/V)) / (1 + ln A)  for 1/A < |x|/V ≤ 1
blocks.where: A is the compression parameter; A = 87.6 is standard in Europe and much of the world. The first segment is linear; the rest is logarithmic.

blocks.text: Both laws make the SQNR roughly constant over a wide range of input levels. Idle-channel noise is the audible quantization noise heard when the talker is silent; with fine steps near zero it is reduced but not eliminated. A-law and μ-law are not compatible, so international calls need conversion.

blocks.text: Companding improves small-signal SNR. It cannot prevent overload when the input exceeds the designed full scale. A shout or a sudden transient still clips at the peak level.

In a uniform system, a sinusoid smaller than full scale by a factor k has signal power k² times smaller, so SQNR falls by 20 log₁₀(1/k) dB. A companded system reduces that fall, but the improvement depends on the law and the code.

Δ²/12 is quantization noise only. Thermal noise, crosstalk and bit errors add separately, so total noise power is the sum of the powers. Some syllabi call non-uniform quantization logarithmic quantization or companded PCM.

items: Use 6.02n + 1.76 dB only for a full-scale sine; for speech use measured active-speech power.
Keep V as peak full scale; Δ = 2V/L uses the full peak-to-peak width.
Do not expect companding to remove clipping; it only reshapes the error at normal levels.

examples.question: An 8-bit uniform PCM system encodes a full-scale sinusoid in the range ±1 V. Find the number of levels, the step size, the quantization noise power, and the SQNR in dB.
steps: Number of levels: L = 2ⁿ with n = 8, so L = 2⁸ = 256 levels.
Full-scale range is from −1 V to +1 V, so the total width is 2V = 2 V. Step: Δ = 2 V / 256 = 0.0078125 V = 7.8125 mV.
Quantization noise power: P_q = Δ²/12 = (0.0078125 V)² / 12 = 6.1035×10⁻⁵ / 12 = 5.0863×10⁻⁶ V².
For a full-scale sine, signal power is V²/2 = (1 V)²/2 = 0.5 V². SQNR = 0.5 / 5.0863×10⁻⁶ = 98,304.
In dB: SQNR_dB = 10 log₁₀(98,304) ≈ 49.9 dB. The shortcut gives 6.02×8 + 1.76 = 49.92 dB; the small difference is rounding in 6.02.
examples.answer: L = 256 levels, Δ = 7.8125 mV, P_q = 5.086×10⁻⁶ V², and SQNR ≈ 49.9 dB.
examples.check:
n = 8
V = 1.0
L = 2 ** n
delta = 2 * V / L
Pq = delta ** 2 / 12
sqnr_db = 6.02 * n + 1.76
print(L)
print(delta)
print(Pq)
print(sqnr_db)

traps: Using 6.02n + 1.76 dB for any signal. It is only for a full-scale sine wave; for speech or arbitrary signals use actual signal power.
Mixing peak V and peak-to-peak 2V. The step is Δ = 2V/L, not V/L.
Claiming companding removes overload. It gives finer steps at low levels but cannot stop clipping beyond full scale.
Treating Δ²/12 as total noise. It is quantization noise only; channel noise, crosstalk and bit errors add separately.
Confusing the compressor with the expander, or swapping the standard values μ = 255 and A = 87.6.

quiz.q: What is quantization, and how many levels does an n-bit uniform quantizer have?
quiz.a: Quantization rounds each sample to one of a finite set of levels. An n-bit uniform quantizer has L = 2ⁿ levels.

quiz.q: Why does non-uniform quantization suit speech better than uniform quantization?
quiz.a: Speech spends much time at small amplitudes, where a small absolute error is audible. Fine steps near zero and coarser steps at peaks give a more even SQNR than one fixed step.

quiz.q: A 10-bit uniform PCM system has a ±2 V range and a full-scale sine input. Find Δ, P_q and the SQNR in dB.
What happens to the SQNR of a small uniform-PCM sine if the step size is doubled while the signal stays the same?
quiz.a: Noise power becomes four times larger, so SQNR falls by 10 log₁₀ 4 ≈ 6 dB.

quiz.q: State the standard μ and A values for 8-bit speech PCM.
quiz.a: μ = 255 for μ-law; A = 87.6 for A-law.

quiz.q: What is idle-channel noise, and how does companding affect it?
quiz.a: It is quantization noise heard during silence. Fine steps near zero reduce it, but they do not remove it completely.

quiz.q: A loud peak exceeds the full-scale range of a companded PCM system. Does companding prevent distortion? Explain.
quiz.a: No. Companding changes step sizes at normal levels; samples beyond full scale are still clipped, producing overload distortion.

beyond: Not for the exam. G.711 still carries μ-law and A-law speech in telephone networks and VoIP gateways. Modern codecs such as Opus and EVS use adaptive prediction and transform coding instead of a fixed companding law. Vector quantization groups several samples into one code and is used in speech and image compression. Search for 'G.711 μ-law', 'A-law segmented PCM' and 'companding in audio' to go further.
